<!-- Generated from stata.Rmd.orig by precompute/precompile.R. Edit the .orig file, not this one. -->



A regression coefficient from observational data is only as credible as the
assumption that no important variable was left out. `sensemakr` (Cinelli &
Hazlett, 2020) makes that assumption concrete: it reports the coefficient you
would have obtained had a variable as strong as one of your observed
covariates been omitted. `bootmakr` adds a standard error, a confidence
interval and a *p*-value for that adjusted coefficient, obtained by
resampling the data the way you would choose standard errors for the
regression itself. This is needed because the usual tools, the impact
threshold of a confounding variable (ITCV) and the analytic interval of
`sensemakr`, break down when the regression calls for robust standard errors
(Lonati & Wulff, 2026); [Why bootstrap?](why-bootstrap.html) shows why. This
page shows a first analysis from start to finish. The same steps in R are in
[Get started in R](bootmakr.html).

## Installation

`bootmakr` builds on the `sensemakr` command, which is on SSC. `bootmakr`
itself is installed from GitHub, and `net get` copies its example data set
into the current folder.

<div class="wrap-code">

```stata
ssc install sensemakr
net install bootmakr, from("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jespernwulff/bootmakr-stata/main/")
net get bootmakr, from("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jespernwulff/bootmakr-stata/main/")
```

</div>

Stata 14 or later is required. To update an existing installation, add the
`replace` option to `net install`. After installation, `help bootmakr` opens
the help file, which is also [on this site](stata-help.html).

## The example data

`firms.dta` is a simulated panel of 250 firms observed for 20 years. Because
the data are simulated, we know the truth: the effect of `x` on `y` is 0.25.
Two firm-level characteristics affect both `x` and `y`, an observed control
`c` and a variable `q` that we pretend not to have. The within-firm
components of `x` and of the disturbance are persistent, so standard errors
must be clustered by firm. (The data are a variant of the simulated example
in Lonati and Wulff, 2026; the R package documents how they were generated.)

```stata
use firms, clear
describe
```

```{.stata-output}
(bootmakr example data: variant of Lonati & Wulff (2026), Table 1)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    name         type    format    label      Variable label
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
firm            long    %12.0g                Firm identifier (cluster)
year            long    %12.0g                Year within firm, 1 to 20
y               double  %10.0g                Outcome
x               double  %10.0g                Predictor of interest; true effect on y is 0.25
c               double  %10.0g                Observed firm-level control
q               double  %10.0g                Unobserved firm-level variable (omitted in the analysis)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Sorted by:
```

Here is the regression a researcher without `q` would run.

```stata
regress y x c, vce(cluster firm)
```

```{.stata-output}
Linear regression                               Number of obs     =      5,000
                                                F(2, 249)         =     191.47
                                                Prob > F          =     0.0000
                                                R-squared         =     0.3635
                                                Root MSE          =        1.1

                                 (Std. err. adjusted for 250 clusters in firm)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
             |               Robust
           y | Coefficient  std. err.      t    P>|t|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
           x |   .4445283   .0405336    10.97   0.000      .364696    .5243607
           c |   .4755564   .0577003     8.24   0.000     .3619135    .5891993
       _cons |    .030529   .0539153     0.57   0.572    -.0756591    .1367171
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```



The coefficient is 0.44 instead of 0.25, because `q` drives both `x`
and `y`. With real data you would not know this. What you can ask is how the
result would change if a variable as strong as something you *do* observe
had been left out. That is the question `bootmakr` answers.

## A first analysis

`sensemakr` needs a *benchmark*: an observed covariate that sets the scale
for the omitted variable. We take `c` and ask what the coefficient of `x`
would be had a variable *as strong as* `c` been omitted. In these data that
is exactly what `q` is.

```stata
bootmakr y x c, treat(x) benchmark(c) cluster(firm) seed(123)
```

```{.stata-output}
Bootstrap results                               Number of obs     =     5,000
                                                Replications      =     1,000

                 (Replications based on 250 clusters in firm)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
             |      Observed    Bootstrap                    Percentile
             |       Coef.      Std. Err.    P-value    [95% Conf. Interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
x            |    .2521337      .0742285      0.0040     .0877736    .3766737
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Note: CI is percentile bootstrap confidence interval
      P-value is bootstrap p-value (H0: x = 0)
      Benchmark: c, kd = 1, ky = 1

Benchmark strength (descriptive; no standard errors involved)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Benchmark: c
                                                 Partial R2    |Partial corr.|
  with x | X                                         0.1433             0.379
  with y | x, X                                      0.1248             0.353
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Implied strength of the omitted variable (sensemakr bounds):
     kd      ky      R2dz.x     R2yz.dx     Impact
   1.00    1.00       0.1673     0.1998      0.222
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Note: R2dz.x (R2yz.dx) = partial R2 of the omitted variable with the
      treatment given the covariates (with the outcome given treatment
      and covariates). Impact = product of its partial correlations with
      the outcome and with the treatment, both given the covariates only:
      the scale of the ITCV; signed so that the omitted variable biases
      the estimate away from zero. Descriptive only: independent of the
      variance estimator, and not a threshold.
```

The command line has the same form as `regress`: the outcome first, then the
treatment and the covariates. The options name the treatment (`treat()`), the
benchmark (`benchmark()`) and, because observations of the same firm are not
independent, the variable that identifies the clusters to resample
(`cluster()`). Everything else is left at its default: an omitted variable
exactly as strong as the benchmark (`kd(1)`) and 1,000 bootstrap
replications. `seed()` makes the result reproducible. The run takes about a
minute. For longer runs, `dots(100)` prints a dot for every 100 replications.

### Reading the output

**The adjusted estimate.** Had a variable as strong as `c` been omitted, the
coefficient of `x` would be 0.252 rather than
0.445. This is the estimate `sensemakr` reports for the same
benchmark, and it is close to the true 0.25. It does not involve the
bootstrap.

**Its uncertainty.** The remaining columns come from the bootstrap. In each
of the 1,000 replications `bootmakr` draws firms with replacement, reruns
`sensemakr` and stores the adjusted estimate. The standard deviation of those
1,000 values is the standard error (0.074), their 2.5th and
97.5th percentiles form the 95 percent confidence interval
(0.088 to 0.377), and the *p*-value
(.004) is twice the smaller of the two shares of
replications that fall on either side of zero. The effect of `x` remains
positive and statistically distinguishable from zero even if an omitted
variable as strong as `c` is at work.

**The benchmark strength.** The second block says what "as strong as `c`"
means: the share of the variance of `x`, and of the variance of `y` that `x`
leaves unexplained, that `c` explains (partial R^2^), and the strength of the
omitted variable these numbers imply, including its *impact*: the product of
its partial correlations with `y` and with `x`, which is the scale on which
the ITCV is stated. All of this is computed from the data. No standard error
is involved, so the block is the same whatever variance estimator you
prefer. See [How strong is the benchmark?](benchmark-strength.html) for the
details.

## From one strength to many: the breakdown point

An omitted variable as strong as `c` does not overturn the result. How much
stronger would it have to be? Give `kd()` several values and `bootmakr`
evaluates each of them on the same bootstrap samples. The `plot` option draws
the result.

```stata
bootmakr y x c, treat(x) benchmark(c) kd(0.5 0.75 1 1.25 1.5) ///
    cluster(firm) seed(123) plot
```

```{.stata-output}

```

![Adjusted estimate and bootstrap 95 percent confidence interval for an omitted variable 0.5 to 1.5 times as strong as c. Solid markers: p < .05.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)



The adjusted estimate shrinks as the assumed omitted variable grows stronger,
and its confidence interval widens. In this run the result holds up to an
omitted variable 1 times as strong as `c` and breaks down at
1.25 times: from there on the interval includes zero. That
*breakdown point* is a compact summary of how robust the finding is.

With several values of `kd()`, the full table is returned in `r(results)`,
with the number of successful replications behind each row, and the implied
strength of the omitted variable in `r(benchmark_strength)`.

```stata
matrix list r(results)
matrix list r(benchmark_strength)
```

## Checking the answer

Simulated data have one advantage over real ones: the omitted variable is in
the file.

```stata
regress y x c q, vce(cluster firm)
```

```{.stata-output}
Linear regression                               Number of obs     =      5,000
                                                F(3, 249)         =     199.21
                                                Prob > F          =     0.0000
                                                R-squared         =     0.4785
                                                Root MSE          =     .99577

                                 (Std. err. adjusted for 250 clusters in firm)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
             |               Robust
           y | Coefficient  std. err.      t    P>|t|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
           x |   .2286068    .036788     6.21   0.000     .1561516    .3010621
           c |    .578841   .0492042    11.76   0.000     .4819316    .6757504
           q |   .5125708   .0486366    10.54   0.000     .4167793    .6083623
       _cons |   .0400548   .0455783     0.88   0.380    -.0497133    .1298229
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```



The coefficient of `x` with `q` in the model, 0.23, lies inside the
bootstrap interval at `kd(1)`. The [Why bootstrap?](why-bootstrap.html)
article uses the same data to show what the ITCV and the analytic interval
of `sensemakr` make of this example.

## The choices you make

**The benchmark.** Choose an observed covariate that is strong and that you
can argue an omitted variable is unlikely to exceed. Report why you chose it.
A group of covariates can serve as a joint benchmark with
`gbenchmark(x1 x2)`.

**The multiple.** `kd()` scales the benchmark's relationship with the
treatment and `ky()` its relationship with the outcome. `ky()` follows `kd()`
unless you set it.

**The resampling scheme.** It should mirror how the data were sampled and how
you would compute standard errors in the regression itself. Without
`cluster()`, observations are resampled, which allows for
heteroskedasticity. With `cluster(id)`, whole clusters are resampled, and
`strata()` requests a stratified bootstrap. See
[Clustered and stratified data](clustering.html).

**Replications and seed.** The default of 1,000 replications is fine for a
first look. For results you report, use more (`reps(5000)` or
`reps(10000)`), set a `seed()`, and when the verdict is close to the
significance threshold check that it has settled with the `converge()`
option.

**Many indicator variables.** Stata re-estimates the regression in every
replication. A model with hundreds of indicator variables (say, one per
village or firm) can take about a second per replication, so start such a
model with a few hundred replications and `dots()` to see how long it will
take.

## Bootstrapping your own program

In standard mode `bootmakr` builds the `sensemakr` call for you. If something
has to happen in every replication before `sensemakr` runs, or you want full
control over the call, write a small e-class program and hand it to
`bootmakr` with `program()`. The program must leave `sensemakr`'s results
behind. `treat()` is then only a label for the output.

```stata
capture program drop my_sens
program define my_sens, eclass
    sensemakr y x c, treat(x) benchmark(c) kd(1) suppress
end

bootmakr, treat(x) program(my_sens) cluster(firm) seed(123)
```

```{.stata-output}
Bootstrap results                               Number of obs     =     5,000
                                                Replications      =     1,000

                 (Replications based on 250 clusters in firm)
                 (Using user-supplied program: my_sens)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
             |      Observed    Bootstrap                    Percentile
             |       Coef.      Std. Err.    P-value    [95% Conf. Interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
x            |    .2521337      .0742285      0.0040     .0877736    .3766737
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Note: CI is percentile bootstrap confidence interval
      P-value is bootstrap p-value (H0: x = 0)

Benchmark strength (descriptive; no standard errors involved)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Implied strength of the omitted variable (sensemakr bounds):
     kd      ky      R2dz.x     R2yz.dx     Impact
   1.00    1.00       0.1673     0.1998      0.222
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Note: R2dz.x (R2yz.dx) = partial R2 of the omitted variable with the
      treatment given the covariates (with the outcome given treatment
      and covariates). Impact = product of its partial correlations with
      the outcome and with the treatment, both given the covariates only:
      the scale of the ITCV; signed so that the omitted variable biases
      the estimate away from zero. Descriptive only: independent of the
      variance estimator, and not a threshold.
```



With the same seed this reproduces the first analysis exactly. In program
mode the benchmark-strength block shows only the implied strength of the
omitted variable, because `bootmakr` does not know which covariate your
program uses as benchmark.
